(...) अदृष्टन् (*adṛṣṭan*) is the form. When the nominative *su* follows, lengthening of the penultimate and elision of *n*. By the rule गतिकारकोप- पदात् कृत् (*gatikārakopa- padāt kṛt*) the accent of the verbal-derivative second member arises.

जंभयन् (*jaṃbhayan*) (root जभि नाशने (*jabhi nāśane*), of the *curādi* class; the suffix *ṇic* in the same sense by the rule printed सत्यापॆ (*satyāpè*); *laṭ* after the *ṇijanta*; the augment *num* because the root is marked *i*; *śatṛ* substituted for *laṭ*; because *śap* is marked *p* and the following sarvadhātuka is unaccented by the rule तास्यनुदात्तेत् (*tāsyanudāttet*), by the accent of *ṇic* the *a* after the *bh* that substituted for it takes the acute); यातुधान्यः (*yātudhānyaḥ*) (the word यातुधानिशब्द (*yātudhāniśabda*); when *jas* follows, *yaṇ* is substituted in the Vedic manner; since *yaṇ* replaces an acute, by the rule उदात्तस्वरितयोर्यणः (*udāttasvaritayoryaṇaḥ*) (पा. सू. ८-२-४ (*pā. sū. 8-2-4*)) a svarita follows the *yaṇ*).

#### Ṛk 9

**॥ संहितापाठः ॥**

> उद॑पस्तद॒सौ [?] सूर्यः॑ पु॒रु विश्वा॑नि॒ जूर्व॑न् ।
> आ॒दि॒त्यः पर्व॑तेभ्यो वि॒श्वदृ॑ष्टो अदृष्ट॒हा ॥ ९ ॥

**॥ पदपाठः ॥**

> उत् । अपप्तत् । असौ । सूर्यः । पुरु । विश्वानि । जूर्वन् ।
> आदित्यः । पर्वतेभ्यः । विश्वदृष्टः । अदृष्टहा ॥ ९ ॥

**॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥**

> असौ पुरस्तादृश्यमानः सूर्यः सर्वस्य प्रेरक आदित्य उदपत्तत् । ऊर्ध्वं
> गच्छति ॥ पततेर्लुजि पुमागमे रूपं ॥ किं कुर्वन् । विश्वानि बहूनि विषाणि पुरु
> प्रभूतं जूर्वन् हिंसन् । कीदृशोऽसौ । पर्वतेभ्यः पर्ववद्भ्यः प्राणिभ्यस्तेषा-
> मुपकारायादित्यो विषोदकादीनामदनशीलः विश्वदृष्टो विश्वं दृष्टं येन
> तादृशः अदृष्टहादृष्टानां विषविशेषाणां हंता । एवंमहानुभावः सूर्यः
> ऊर्ध्वमारोहति । अतो विषशंका न कार्या ॥

*Gist:* The sun, rising, destroys many poisons for the benefit of creatures; all-seeing and destroyer of the unseen; so fear of poison is needless.

**प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)**

पर्वतेभ्यः—प्राणिगळ उपकारक्कागि (*parvatebhyaḥ—prāṇigaḷa upakārakkāgi*) (for the benefit of creatures). अदित्यः—विषोदकादिगळन्नु हीरुव आदित्य रूपनू (*adityaḥ—viṣodakādigaḷannu hīruva āditya rūpanū*) (the Āditya form that absorbs poison, water and the like). विश्वदृष्टिः—सकलवन्नू नोडतक्कवनू (*viśvadṛṣṭiḥ—sakalavannū noḍatakkavanū*) (the one who sees everything). अदृष्टहा—सूक्ष्मवाद विषचरगळन्नु (*adṛṣṭahā—sūkṣmavāda viṣacaragaḷannu*) (of the destroyer of subtle poison-bearers; the entry is interrupted here by the notes below and the page boundary).

*[As supplied, a stray line [23]Vol. 14. (*[23]Vol. 14.*) stands inside the Pratipadārtha, followed by the unmarked running head of printed p. 354; both are kept as italic notes in the Kannada text.]*

### Printed p. 354

*Running head (unmarked in the supplied text, as printed): 354 रायणभाष्यसहिता [ मं. १. अ. २४. सू. १९१ (*354 rāyaṇabhāṣyasahitā [ maṃ. 1. a. 24. sū. 191*).*

नाशमाडुववनू आद (*nāśamāḍuvavanū āda*) (the entry continues: destroying). आसौ सूर‍्यः—ई सूर‍्यनु (*āsau sūryaḥ—ī sūryanu*) (this sun). विश्वानि—समस्तवाद विषगळन्नू (*viśvāni—samastavāda viṣagaḷannū*) (all the poisons). पुरु— पूर्णवागि (*puru— pūrṇavāgi*) (completely). जूर्वन्—नाशमाडुत्ता (*jūrvan—nāśamāḍuttā*) (destroying). उदपप्तत्—उदयिसि मेलक्कॆ बरुत्तानॆ. (*udapaptat—udayisi melakkè baruttānè.*) (rises up on high).

**भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)**

The sun, the Āditya form that absorbs poison, water and the like for the benefit of creatures, who sees everything and destroys subtle poison-bearers, rises up on high, destroying completely all the poisons (the supplied text reads सूरनु (*sūranu*) for the sun in this line).

**Printed English translation**

The Sun has risen on high, destroying all the many (poisons) ; Aditya, the all-seeing, the destroyer of the unseen, (rises) for (the good of) living benigs.

*(The printed English reads "benigs" for "beings", as supplied.)*

**Viśeṣaviṣayagaḷu (Special Topics, Ṛk 9)**

In the previous ṛk the rising of the sun, and thereby the flight of the wicked creatures, were mentioned; in this ṛk it is explained how the sun gradually climbs higher, and how by the sharpness of its rays that arises therefrom, poisons and the like are destroyed.

सूर्यः—सर्वस्य प्रेरक आदित्यः (*sūryaḥ—sarvasya preraka ādityaḥ*): the sun who impels the whole world, that is, all the creatures in the world. If we did not receive the heat that comes from the sun through its rays, we could not live. As said in ऋ. सं. १-११५-१ (*ṛ. saṃ. 1-115-1*), सूर्य आत्मा जगतः (*sūrya ātmā jagataḥ*), the sun himself is the soul of the whole world. Without the brilliance of the sun not even a blade of grass on the earth could move. For the whole class of creatures and for men the brilliance (heat) of the sun is absolutely necessary. Since heat (fire) is one of the five elements, the brilliance of the sun is necessary just as air, water and food are necessary. There is a difference between the brilliance that arises from fire and the like and the brilliance of the sun. The brilliance of the sun has the power to remove poison and to produce health. Therefore it is said here, by the sentence पुरु विश्वानि विषाणि जूर्वन-हिंसन् (*puru viśvāni viṣāṇi jūrvana-hiṃsan*), that the sharp rays of the midday sun destroy poison. Earlier the sage प्रसृण्वऋषियु (*prasṛṇvaṛṣiyu*) (as printed) prayed:

हृद्रोगं मम सूर्य हरिमाणं च नाशय । (*hṛdrogaṃ mama sūrya harimāṇaṃ ca nāśaya |*)
(य. सं. १-५०-११) (*(ya. saṃ. 1-50-11)*)

(The reference is printed य. सं. (*ya. saṃ.*), as supplied.) "O sun, destroy the disease that has spread in my heart and the yellow colour caused by leprosy that has spread over my skin (तॊन्नु. Leprosy (*tònnu. Leprosy*))": this prayer is an illustration of the sun's power to remove disease.

पर्वतेभ्यः—पर्ववद्भ्यः प्राणिभ्यस्तेषामुपकारायादित्यो विषोदकादी- नामदनशीलः उदपस्तत् (*parvatebhyaḥ—parvavadbhyaḥ prāṇibhyasteṣāmupakārāyādityo viṣodakādī- nāmadanaśīlaḥ udapastat*) (as printed): Sāyaṇa has explained the word *parvata* as creatures with bodies like joints (गिण्णुगळंतॆ (*giṇṇugaḷaṃtè*)); that is, the different parts of the body, foot, knee, thigh, belly, neck and head, together form one big thing; likewise on a *parvata* (hill) many rocks lie one over another and all of them together bear the name *parvata*. That example is here compared to the bodies of creatures. And the words "for doing good to such creatures" have been supplied to complete the sense of the sentence.

*Gist:* The sage places the poison in the sun's disc, like a wine-bag in a distiller's house; neither sun nor we die; honey-lore makes it nectar.

*[As supplied, a line reading प्रपदार्थ (*prapadārtha*) stands inside the bhāṣya block where the Pratipadārtha label belongs; the following lines carry block marks in the supplied text and are given as prose; standard label inserted.]*

**प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)**

सुरावतः—सुरॆयन्नु ( मद्यवन्नु ) तयारिसतक्कवन मनॆयल्लि (*surāvataḥ—surèyannu ( madyavannu ) tayārisatakkavana manèyalli*) (in the house of one who prepares liquor (wine)). दृतिं इव—सुरॆ यन्नु तुंबुव चीलवन्नु इडुवंतॆ (*dṛtiṃ iva—surè yannu tuṃbuva cīlavannu iḍuvaṃtè*) (as one places the bag in which liquor is filled). विषं—नम्म सुत्तलू व्यापिसिरुव विषवन्नु (*viṣaṃ—namma suttalū vyāpisiruva viṣavannu*) (the poison spread around us). सूर‍्यॆ— सूर‍्य मंडलदल्लि (बिसलिनल्लि) (*sūryè— sūrya maṃḍaladalli (bisalinalli)*) (in the disc of the sun (in the sunshine)). आ सजामि—संयोजिसुत्तेनॆ, (इडुत्तेनॆ) (*ā sajāmi—saṃyojisuttenè, (iḍuttenè)*) (I join, I place). सो चित्—पूज्य नाद आ सूर‍्यनादरो (*so cit—pūjya nāda ā sūryanādaro*) (that revered sun, however). नु—खंडितवागियू (*nu—khaṃḍitavāgiyū*) (certainly). न मराति—मरणवन्नु हॊंदुवुदिल्ल (*na marāti—maraṇavannu hòṃduvudilla*) (does not die). नो वयं मराम—अवन अनुग्रहदिंद नावू मरणवन्नु हॊंदुवुदिल्ल (*no vayaṃ marāma—avana anugrahadiṃda nāvū maraṇavannu hòṃduvudilla*) (by his favour we too do not die). आरे-दूरदल्लिद्दरू सह (*āre-dūradalliddarū saha*) (even though far away). हरिष्ठाः—अश्वगळ मेलॆ आरूढनागिरुव सूर‍्यनु (*hariṣṭhāḥ—aśvagaḷa melè ārūḍhanāgiruva sūryanu*) (the sun mounted on horses). अस्य—ई विषद (*asya—ī viṣada*) (of this poison). योजनं—संपर्क वन्नु हॊंदिदनु (ई विषद शक्तियु ननगॆ प्रसरिसदंतॆ माडिदनु) (ऎलै विषवे) (*yojanaṃ—saṃparka vannu hòṃdidanu (ī viṣada śaktiyu nanagè prasarisadaṃtè māḍidanu) (èlai viṣave)*) (came into contact (made the force of this poison not spread to me) (O poison)). मधुला— मधुविद्यॆयु (*madhulā— madhuvidyèyu*) (the honey-lore). त्वा—निन्नन्नु (*tvā—ninnannu*) (you). मधु चकार—अमृतवन्नागि परिवर्तिसिदॆ (*madhu cakāra—amṛtavannāgi parivartisidè*) (turned into nectar).

**भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)**

As one places the bag in which liquor is filled in the house of one who prepares liquor, I place the poison spread around us in the disc of the sun. That revered sun, however, certainly does not die; by his favour we too do not die. Even though far away, the sun mounted on horses came into contact with this poison and made its force not spread to us. O poison, the honey-lore has turned you into nectar.

**Printed English translation**

I deposit the poison in the solar orb, like a leather bottle in the house of a vender of spirits : verily, that adorable (Sun) never dies, nor, (through his favour), shall we die (of the venom) ; for, through afar off, yet drawn by his coursers, he will overtake (the poison) ; the science of antidotes converted you, (Poison), to ambrosia,

**Viśeṣaviṣayagaḷu (Special Topics, Ṛk 10)**

In the preceding ṛks the rising of the sun and the sun's ascent were spoken of; in this ṛk the way in which the sun removes poison is explained.

The bhāṣyakāra says: आदित्य- मंडले चतुर्थेनांगुलिना विषमादाय मधुकृत्य योजयित्वा निर्विषो भवेदिति यदेतद्विषविद्यायामुक्तं तदिदमत्तोच्यते (*āditya- maṃḍale caturthenāṃgulinā viṣamādāya madhukṛtya yojayitvā nirviṣo bhavediti yadetadviṣavidyāyāmuktaṃ tadidamattocyate*). That is: with the fourth finger of the right hand, that is, the finger called अनामिका (*anāmikā*), the poison in the wound is taken out and placed in the solar orb (in a figure drawn to resemble the orb of the sun, in the sunshine); and if the procedures with the *madhuvidyā* are performed, the poison is removed; what is said in the work called विषविद्य (*viṣavidya*) is told here: thus the bhāṣyakāra has explained the main subject of this ṛk.

सूरै विषं आ सजामि—विषावृतोऽगस्योऽहं सूरै सर्वस्य प्रेरयितरि मधुविद्यारूपे सूरमंडले विषमावृत्य वर्तमानं सूर आ सजामि (*sūrai viṣaṃ ā sajāmi—viṣāvṛto 'gasyo 'haṃ sūrai sarvasya prerayitari madhuvidyārūpe sūramaṃḍale viṣamāvṛtya vartamānaṃ sūra ā sajāmi*) (as supplied, with the conjunct of *ry* lost in *sūrya* in the words printed सूरै (*sūrai*), सूरमंडले (*sūramaṃḍale*), सूर (*sūra*)): I, Agastya, whose body is filled with poison, collect and place all the poison (in my body) in the solar orb which has the form of the *madhuvidyā* that impels the whole world; so the sage Agastya has said. Here "solar orb" may mean something like a solar orb in the sunshine in the procedures performed for the removal of poison (or, according to the *mantra-tantra* science, a solar-orb figure formed of seed syllables). Mainly it can be said: in a place with the rays of the sun, or in the sunshine.

दृतिं सुरावतो गृहे (*dṛtiṃ surāvato gṛhe*): the sage has given an example for the matter of collecting the poison and placing it in the sunshine:

सुरावतो गृहे सुरानिर्मातृसदने दृतिमिव चर्ममयं सुरापात्रमिन (*surāvato gṛhe surānirmātṛsadane dṛtimiva carmamayaṃ surāpātramina*) (as printed) । यथा तत्कर्तुर्न दोषाय भवति तद्वद्विषमादित्यस्य न बाधकमित्यर्थः (*yathā tatkarturna doṣāya bhavati tadvadviṣamādityasya na bādhakamityarthaḥ*): as a man who makes liquor stores the liquor in a leather bag in his house, I too take out all the poison and place it in one place in the sunshine (the sentence continues on the next page).

### Printed p. 358

*Running head (as supplied): [358 सायणभाष्यसहिता । मं. १. अ. २४. सू. १९०] (*[358 sāyaṇabhāṣyasahitā | maṃ. 1. a. 24. sū. 190]*), as printed, with the sūkta number ೧೯೦ although the page belongs to Sūkta 191.*

so the sage gives the simile. And as, by thus collecting liquor and placing it in one place (without drinking it), no harm of any kind arises to that liquor-maker, so, it is described, no harm arises to the sun from the poison collection placed in the sunshine.

चित्—चिदिति पूजायां । अत्यंतमविनश्वरा (*cit—ciditi pūjāyāṃ | atyaṃtamavinaśvarā*): Yāska says that the particle *cit* is used in many kinds of meaning: चिदि- त्येषोऽनेककर्मा (*cidi- tyeṣo 'nekakarmā*); and आचार्यश्चिदिदं ब्रूयादिति पूजायां । दधिचिदित्युपमार्थे! कुल्माषांश्चिद्वाहरेत्यवकुत्सिते (*ācāryaścididaṃ brūyāditi pūjāyāṃ | dadhicidityupamārthe! kulmāṣāṃścidvāharetyavakutsite*) (as printed). In the sentence *ācāryaś cit* the particle *cit* is used in the sense of worship; in *dadhi cit* in the sense of comparison; in *kulmāṣāṃś cit* in a censuring sense; having given examples in this way, he explained the meaning. Here Sāyaṇa has explained it as used in the sense of worship.

सो चिन्नु न मराति नो वयं (*so cinnu na marāti no vayaṃ*): for this sentence Sāyaṇa says पूज्यः सः सूर‍्यः खलु न मराति । न म्रियते । नो वयं मराम । तदनुग्रहात्तत्रैव विषस्य योजितत्वा द्वयमपि न म्रियामहै (*pūjyaḥ saḥ sūryaḥ khalu na marāti | na mriyate | no vayaṃ marāma | tadanugrahāttatraiva viṣasya yojitatvā dvayamapi na mriyāmahai*). Since the poison is placed in the sunshine, there is no harm to the sun; therefore the sun does not die, and we do not die. The main purport is that since the sun has the power to take away poison, no evil befalls the sun from the poison we place in the sunshine; by the grace of that sun our poison is removed and no evil befalls us either, that is, we too do not die. The reason for this will be told in the next sentence.

अस्य योजनं हरिष्ठा चकार (*asya yojanaṃ hariṣṭhā cakāra*): even though the sun is very far away, with the help of his rays he absorbs the poison and makes it powerless. And the poison goes and becomes nectar; this the sage says here, addressing the poison itself.

मधु त्वा मधुला चकार (*madhu tvā madhulā cakāra*) — विषस्य विषभावं दूरेऽपनोद्यामृतीचकारेति । एष्यव मधुना मधुदात्रि निर्विषीकर्त्रि मधुविद्या । यदेतदादित्यस्य विषयोजनं तेन चामृतीकरणं यदस्ति एषा मधुविद्या (*viṣasya viṣabhāvaṃ dūre 'panodyāmṛtīcakāreti | eṣyava madhunā madhudātri nirviṣīkartri madhuvidyā | yadetadādityasya viṣayojanaṃ tena cāmṛtīkaraṇaṃ yadasti eṣā madhuvidyā*) (as printed, *ēṣyava madhunā* against the bhāṣya's reading). To place the poison in the solar orb, and the sun making that poison into nectar, is what is called *madhuvidyā*. Therefore the sage, addressing the poison, says: O poison, the sun not only makes your poison (your power to kill) powerless, but also converts the poison into nectar by the *madhuvidyā*.

In this matter the scholar Wilson ऎंब पंडितनु (*Wilson èṃba paṃḍitanu*) ("Wilson") has said:

> The notion that pervades this stanza and forms the burden of the three following, is derived, according to Sayana, from the Visha-Vidya, the science of poisonns or of antidotes,

### Printed p. 359

*Running head (as supplied): [अ. २. अ. ५. व. १५. । ऋग्वेदसंहिता 359] (*[a. 2. a. 5. va. 15. | ṛgvedasaṃhitā 359]*).*

> whence it is also termed Madhu-vidya, science of ambrosia; one formula of which, as cited by him is—"having taken the poison in the solar arb with the fourth finger; having made it ambrosia and caused them to blend together, may it become poisonous" By the Surya Mandala or orb of the Sun is probably to be understood a mystical diagram or figure wholly or partly typical of the solar orb; the Sun being considered as especially instrumental in counteracting the operation of poison ; the science of antidotes is also named iu the text Madhula, as synonymous with Madhuvidya. It was origiually taught by Indra to Dadyanch who communicated it to the aswins, and thereby lost his head.

*[The English quotation of the supplied text contains machine-reading slips, such as "poisonns", "arb", "iu" and "origiually"; it is reproduced as supplied, divided by the page boundary.]*

ऎंदु हेळिरुवनु (*èṃdu heḷiruvanu*): so he has said. The science that destroys poison and turns it into nectar is called *madhuvidyā*. In this ṛk that word *madhuvidyā* is conveyed by the word *madhulā*. It is said that this *madhuvidyā* was taught formerly by Indra to Dadhīci with the condition that it should not be told to anyone, and that if it were told to anyone against this, the head of the one who told it would be cut off. Yet at the prayer of the Aśvin gods the sage Dadhīci taught that *madhuvidyā* to them, and as a result his head was cut off, and in place of that head the Aśvin gods fixed a horse's head and revived him; the details of this story we have described at length in ऋ. सं. भाग ५ पेजु 615 ; भाग 6 पेजु 615 ; भाग ९ पेजु 245 मत्तु 401 (*ṛ. saṃ. bhāga 5 peju 615 ; bhāga 6 peju 615 ; bhāga 9 peju 245 mattu 401*) and other places.

**Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā** (grammar page for Ṛk 10, noted briefly; the supplied text ends within it)

The page explains: सजामि (*sajāmi*) (root षण्ण संगे (*ṣaṇṇa saṃge*); since the Veda has a change of vikaraṇa, *śa* in place of *śap* in the present; because it behaves as if marked *j*, elision of the penultimate nasal; lengthening of the stem by the rule अतोदीर्घो- यञ् (*atodīrgho- yañ*); the verbal *nighāta* accent); दृतिम् (*dṛtim*) (root द्वि विदारणे (*dvi vidāraṇe*), as printed; the suffix *ti* by the rule दृणातेर्ह्रस्वश्च (*dṛṇāterhrasvaśca*) (उ. सू. ६२३ (*u. sū. 623*)); the root is shortened; because it is marked *n* by the rule पदिप्रथिभ्यां नित् (*padiprathibhyāṃ nit*), an acute on the first syllable by the rule printed इत्यादि- निर्त्यम् (*ityādi- nirtyam*)); मराति (*marāti*) (root मृज् प्राणत्यागे (*mṛj prāṇatyāge*), as printed; by *vyatyaya* the parasmaipada suffix also arises; the augment *aṭ* for the *tip* of the *leṭ* by the rule लेटोऽडाट् (*leṭo 'ḍāṭ*); *guṇa* of the root's *ṛ*; the verbal *nighāta* accent because it follows a verb form); मराम (*marāma*) (the same root; *leṭ*, first person plural; the accent operations as before); हरिष्ठाः (*hariṣṭhāḥ*) (हरिसु तिष्ठतीति हरिष्ठाः (*harisu tiṣṭhatīti hariṣṭhāḥ*); the root ष्ठा गतिनिवृत्तौ (*ṣṭhā gatinivṛttau*); the suffix *ka* by the rule सुपिस्थः (*supisthaḥ*) (पा सू. ३-२-४ (*pā sū. 3-2-4*)); elision of the root's *ā* by the rule आतोलोप इटिच (*ātolopa iṭica*)).

### Printed p. 360

*Running head (as supplied): [360 सायणभाष्यसहिता [मं. १. अ. २४. सू. १९१] (*[360 sāyaṇabhāṣyasahitā [maṃ. 1. a. 24. sū. 191]*).*

*(Continuation of the grammar page of Ṛk 10 of Sūkta 191, from the end of the previous window.)*

By *vyatyaya* the plural suffix has come. By the rule गतिकारकोप (*gatikārakopa*) the accent of the verbal-derivative second member arises. मधुला (*madhulā*) (root ला आदाने (*lā ādāne*); since in the rule सुपिस्थः (*supisthaḥ*) the word सुपि (*supi*) is divided as a separate rule, the suffix *ka* also comes after other roots ending in *ā* when a case-ended word is the upapada, so the suffix *ka* here too; as before the accent of the second member arises).

Three readings of the Pada (one in Ṛk 11 and two in Ṛk 12) are marked with a query, as they differ from the Saṃhitā.]*

#### Ṛk 11

**॥ संहितापाठः ॥**

> इ॒य॒त्ति॒का श॑कुंति॒का स॒का ज॑घास ते वि॒षं ।
> सो चि॒न्नु न म॑राति॒ नो व॒यं म॑रामा॒रे अ॑स्य॒ योज॑नं
> हरि॒ष्ठा मधु॑ त्वा मधु॒ला च॑कार ॥ ११ ॥

**॥ पदपाठः ॥**

> इयत्तिका । शकुंतिका । सका । जघास । ते । विषं ।
> सो इति । चित् । नु । न । मराति । नो इति । वयं । मराम । आरे । अस्य ।
> योजनं । हरिस्थाः [?] । मधु । त्वा । मधुला । चकार ॥ ११ ॥

**॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥**

> इयत्तिका । इयत्तां कुर्वाणेयत्तावती वा । बालेत्यर्थः । शकुंतिका !
> शकुंतः शकुनः ! तस्य स्त्री । तां कपिंजलीमाहुः । सका सा ते तव विषं जघास ।
> भक्षितवती । सा विषहर्त्रिति प्रसिद्धा । सो चित् ॥ सा उ इति निपातसमुदाय एकं
> पदं !! सापि शकुंतिका न म्रियते नित्यप्रतिपक्षत्वाद्विषस्य । शिष्टं व्याख्यातचरं । अनेन
> विद्यायां यद्देहावृतं विषं तस्य शकुनेभ्य आदित्याय च प्रदानमस्तीत्युक्तं भवति!!

*Gist:* The little female partridge eats your poison and does not die; nor do we; the far sun neutralises it; honey-lore makes it nectar.

**प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)**

इयत्तिका—ई सण्ण रूपद (*iyattikā—ī saṇṇa rūpada*) (of this small form). सका शकुंतिका—अदे पक्षियु (*sakā śakuṃtikā—ade pakṣiyu*) (that same bird). ते—निन्न (*te—ninna*) (your). विषं— विषवन्नु (*viṣaṃ— viṣavannu*) (poison). जघास—भक्षिसिदॆ (आदरू सह) (*jaghāsa—bhakṣisidè (ādarū saha)*) (has eaten, even so). सो चित्—शक्तियुतवाद अदु (*so cit—śaktiyutavāda adu*) (that powerful one). नु—खंडित वागियू (*nu—khaṃḍita vāgiyū*) (certainly). न मराति—मरणवन्नु हॊंदुवुदिल्ल (*na marāti—maraṇavannu hòṃduvudilla*) (does not die). नो वयं मराम—नावू सह मृत (*no vayaṃ marāma—nāvū saha mṛta*) (we also do not die: the entry is divided across the page boundary).

### Printed p. 361

*Running head (as supplied): [अ. २. अ. ५. व. १६.] ऋग्वेदसंहिता 361 (*[a. 2. a. 5. va. 16.] ṛgvedasaṃhitā 361*).*

रागुवुदिल्ल (*rāguvudilla*) (the rest of the entry). आरे—दूरदल्लिद्दरू सह (*āre—dūradalliddarū saha*) (though far away). हरिष्ठाः—अश्वारूढनाद सूर्यनु (*hariṣṭhāḥ—aśvārūḍhanāda sūryanu*) (the sun mounted on horses). अस्य—ई विषद (*asya—ī viṣada*) (of this poison). योजनं—संपर्कवन्नु हॊंदुत्तानॆ (*yojanaṃ—saṃparkavannu hòṃduttānè*) (comes into contact). (ई विषद शक्तियु नमगॆ प्रसरिसदंतॆ माडुत्तानॆ) (*(ī viṣada śaktiyu namagè prasarisadaṃtè māḍuttānè)*) (makes the force of this poison not spread to us). ( ऎलै विषवे ) मधुला—मधुविद्यॆयु (*( èlai viṣave ) madhulā—madhuvidyèyu*) (O poison, the honey-lore). त्वा—निन्नन्नु (*tvā—ninnannu*) (you). मधु चकार—अमृतवन्नागि परिवर्तिसिदॆ (*madhu cakāra—amṛtavannāgi parivartisidè*) (has turned into nectar).

**भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)**

This small bird has eaten your poison; yet, being powerful, it does not die. Even though far away, the sun mounted on horses comes into contact with this poison and makes the force of the poison not spread to us (the supplied text reads सूरनु (*sūranu*) for the sun in this line). O poison, the honey-lore has turned you into nectar.

**Printed English translation**

That little insignificant bird has swallowed your venom ; she does not die, nor shall we die; for, although afar off, yet drawn by his coursers, (the Sun) will overtake (the poison) ; the science of antidotes has converted you (Poison), to ambrosia.

**Viśeṣaviṣayagaḷu (Special Topics, Ṛk 11)**

In the previous ṛk it was said that, since he is in the solar orb, the sun removes poison; now it is described that a bird called कपिंजल (*kapiṃjala*) eats poison and removes it.

इयत्तिका शकुंतिका । इयत्तां कुर्वाणेयत्तावती वा । बालेत्यर्थः (*iyattikā śakuṃtikā | iyattāṃ kurvāṇeyattāvatī vā | bāletyarthaḥ*): it is the nature of children to see what someone does and imitate it. Therefore *iyattikā* means a girl (of an imitating nature). शकुंतः (*śakuṃtaḥ*) means the bird शकुन (*śakuna*), or it is also named कपिंजल (*kapiṃjala*) (Francoline partridge (*Francoline partridge*)). शकुंतिका (*śakuṃtikā*) means a female bird. Therefore *iyattikā-śakuntikā* means the small female young of the *śakuna* or *kapiñjala* bird. The name of the bird *śakunta* is mentioned in ऋ. सं. २-४२-३, २-४३-१ (*ṛ. saṃ. 2-42-3, 2-43-1*).

सका जघास ते विषं (*sakā jaghāsa te viṣaṃ*): सका (*sakā*) means the same as सा (*sā*). The young of the female *kapiñjala* bird explained before ate (swallowed) your poison (the poison of the poison-bearer); a bird so small eats poison without minding it; since that is its natural food, it does not die; we too do not die; and so on, all the details are as before.

### Printed p. 362

*Running head (as supplied): [362 सायणभाष्यसहिता [ मं. १ अ. २४. सू १९१] (*[362 sāyaṇabhāṣyasahitā [ maṃ. 1 a. 24. sū 191]*).*

सो चिन्नु (*so cinnu*): here the bhāṣyakāra has not divided the words as सः चित् नु (*saḥ cit nu*), as he did in the previous ṛk. Instead the word division is सा+उ=सो (*sā+u=so*). Since the particle उ ऎंब निपातवु (*u èṃba nipātavu*) is used to fill out the word, he has explained that if the division सा (*sā*) is made, the meaning fits as an adjective of the word शकुंतिका (*śakuṃtikā*).

**Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā** (grammar page for Ṛk 11, noted briefly)

The page explains: सका (*sakā*) (the word *tad*; by the rule पा. सू. ५-३-७१ (*pā. sū. 5-3-71*) the *akac* comes in the middle; by the rule तदोःसाव (*tadoḥsāva*) the initial *t* is replaced by *s*; since *akac* is marked *c*, the acute on the end by the rule चितः (*citaḥ*); because the stem ends in *a*, टाप् (*ṭāp*) in the feminine; by the single substitute that too takes the acute); जघास (*jaghāsa*) (root अद भक्षणे (*ada bhakṣaṇe*); when the perfect is intended, by the rule लिट्यन्यतरस्याम् (*liṭyanyatarasyām*) (पा. सू २-४-४० (*pā. sū 2-4-40*)) the root takes the substitute printed घस् ल्आ (*ghas lā*); reduplication and so on; lengthening of the penultimate by the rule अतउपधायाः (*ataupadhāyāḥ*); the *nighāta* accent because it follows a verb form); सो इति (*so iti*) (here there are two words, सा उ (*sā u*); since these are read in the rule निपाताः (*nipātāḥ*), both receive the name *nipāta* and form a single word).

#### Ṛk 12

**॥ संहितापाठः ॥**

> त्रिः स॒प्त वि॑ष्णुलिंग॒का वि॒षस्य॒ पुष्प॑मक्षन् ।
> ताश्चि॒न्नु न म॑रंति॒ नो व॒यं म॑रामा॒रे अ॑स्य॒ योज॑नं
> हरि॒ष्ठा मधु॑ त्वा मधु॒ला च॑कार ॥ १२ ॥

**॥ पदपाठः ॥**

> त्रिः । सप्त । विष्णुलिंगकाः । विषस्य । पुष्यं [?] । अक्षन् ।
> ताः । चित् । नु । न । मरंति । नो इति । वयं । मराम । आरे । अस्य । योजनं ।
> हरिस्थाः [?] । मधु । त्वा । मधुला । चकार ॥ १२ ॥

### Printed p. 363

*Running head (as supplied): [अ २ अ. ५. व. १६] ऋग्वेदसंहिता 363 (*[a 2 a. 5. va. 16] ṛgvedasaṃhitā 363*).*

*(Continuation of Ṛk 12 of Sūkta 191, after its Saṃhitā and Pada.)*

**॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥**

> त्रिः सप्त त्रिगुणिताः सप्तसंख्याका विष्णुलिंगका विविधाः विष्णुलिंगकाः । सप्तसु
> जह्वासु लोहितशुक्लकृष्णभेदेनैकविंशतिर्यासां ताः । यद्वा । त्रिः सप्तैकविंशति-
> भेदा विष्णुलिंगकाः सूक्ष्मचटकिका विषप्रतिपक्षभूताः । विषस्यास्मदावरकस्य पुष्यं
> पोषमक्षन् । अदंतु नाशयंतु । ताश्च न मरंति न वयमपि । शिष्टमवशिष्टं ॥

*Gist:* Twenty-one kinds of tiny poison-opposing creatures (fire-sparks or small birds) consume the strength of the poison; they do not die, nor do we.

**प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)**

त्रिः सप्त—त्रिगुणितवाद सप्तसंख्याकवुळ्ळ (२१) ऎंदरॆ इप्पत्तॊंदु (*triḥ sapta—triguṇitavāda saptasaṃkhyākavuḷḷa (21) èṃdarè ippattòṃdu*) (thrice seven, that is, twenty-one). विष्णुलिंगका:— विधविधवाद अग्निकॆंडगळु (*viṣṇuliṃgakā:— vidhavidhavāda agnikèṃḍagaḷu*) (various fire-sparks). विषस्य—नम्मन्नु आवरिसिरुव विषद (*viṣasya—nammannu āvarisiruva viṣada*) (of the poison that envelops us). पुष्यं—प्रबलवाद शक्तियन्नु (*puṣyaṃ—prabalavāda śaktiyannu*) (the strong force). अक्षन्—नुंगिबिडलि (नाशमाडलि) (*akṣan—nuṃgibiḍali (nāśamāḍali)*) (may they swallow (destroy)). ताश्चिन्नु—अवुगळादरो (*tāścinnu—avugaḷādaro*) (those, however). न मराति—खंडितवागियू मरणवन्नु हॊंदुवुदिल्ल (*na marāti—khaṃḍitavāgiyū maraṇavannu hòṃduvudilla*) (certainly do not die). नो वयं मराम—नावू मृतियन्नु हॊंदुवुदिल्ल (*no vayaṃ marāma—nāvū mṛtiyannu hòṃduvudilla*) (nor do we die). आरे— दूरदल्लिद्दरू सह (*āre— dūradalliddarū saha*) (even though far away). हरिष्ठाः—अश्वारूढनागिरुव सूर‍्यनु (*hariṣṭhāḥ—aśvārūḍhanāgiruva sūryanu*) (the sun mounted on horses). अस्य—ई विषद (*asya—ī viṣada*) (of this poison). योजनं— संपर्कवन्नु हॊंदिदनु (ई विषद शक्तियु नमगॆ प्रसरिसदंतॆ माडिदनु) (*yojanaṃ— saṃparkavannu hòṃdidanu (ī viṣada śaktiyu namagè prasarisadaṃtè māḍidanu)*) (came into contact (made the force of this poison not spread to us)). मधुला—मधु विद्यॆयु (*madhulā—madhu vidyèyu*) (the honey-lore). त्वा—निन्नन्नु (*tvā—ninnannu*) (you). मधु चकार—अमृतवन्नागि परिवर्तिसिदॆ. (*madhu cakāra—amṛtavannāgi parivartisidè.*) (has turned into nectar).

**भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)**

May the twenty-one kinds of fire-sparks, of various kinds, swallow and destroy the strong force of the poison that envelops us. They have no death. By their influence we too do not die. Even though far away, the sun mounted on horses came into contact with this poison and made its force not spread to us. O poison, the honey-lore has turned you into nectar.

**Printed English translation**

May the thrice-seven sparks (of Agni) consume the influence of the venom; they verily do not perish ; nor shall we die; for although afar off, the Sun, drawn by his coursers, will overtake the poison; the science of antidotes has converted you, (Poison), to ambrosia.

*[As supplied, the label line of the Special Topics reads विशेषविवरगळु (*viśeṣavivaragaḷu*), run on after the printed English; standard label inserted.]*

**Viśeṣaviṣayagaḷu (Special Topics, Ṛk 12)**

In this ṛk it is prayed that the twenty-one kinds of particles or birds of Agni may remove our poison.

त्रिः सप्त—त्रिगुणिताः सप्तसंख्याका (*triḥ sapta—triguṇitāḥ saptasaṃkhyākā*): three times seven, or twenty-one, is the meaning.

### Printed p. 364

*Running head (as supplied): [364 सायणभाष्यसहिता [ मं. १. अ. २४. सू १९१] (*[364 sāyaṇabhāṣyasahitā [ maṃ. 1. a. 24. sū 191]*).*

विष्णुलिंगकाः—विविधाः विष्णुलिंगकाः । सप्तसु जिह्वासु लोहितशुक्लकृष्णभेदे- नैकविंशतिर्यासां ताः । यद्वा । त्रिःसप्तैकविंशतिभेदा विष्णुलिंगका सूक्ष्मचटकिका विषप्रतिपक्षभूताः (*viṣṇuliṃgakāḥ—vividhāḥ viṣṇuliṃgakāḥ | saptasu jihvāsu lohitaśuklakṛṣṇabhede- naikaviṃśatiryāsāṃ tāḥ | yadvā | triḥsaptaikaviṃśatibhedā viṣṇuliṃgakā sūkṣmacaṭakikā viṣapratipakṣabhūtāḥ*) (as printed): it is said that the particles of Agni are of twenty-one kinds. That Agni has seven tongues, that is, seven flames (Flames (*Flames*)), is well known. In each flame there are twenty-one particles with the distinctions red, white and black. Or, *viṣṇuliṅga* means sparrows or the small birds called गरुडपक्षि (*garuḍapakṣi*) (as printed); among them there are twenty-one varieties or kinds; they are of the nature of eating poison without minding it. The other matters are as in the previous ṛk.

**Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā** (grammar page for Ṛk 12, noted briefly)

The page explains: पुष्यम् (*puṣyam*) (root पुष पुष्टौ (*puṣa puṣṭau*); the Vedic suffix printed श प्रत्यय (*śa pratyaya*); because it is marked *ś*, when it follows, the vikaraṇa *śyan*; because it is marked *n*, the acute on the first syllable); अक्षन् (*akṣan*) (root आद भक्षणे (*āda bhakṣaṇe*), as printed; *luṅ* in the sense of the imperative in the Veda; by the rule पा. सू. २-४-३७ (*pā. sū. 2-4-37*) the root takes the substitute printed घस्ल्य (*ghaslya*); by the rule मंत्रेघस (*maṃtreghasa*) *luk* for *cli*; by the rule गहमन (*gahamana*) elision of the penultimate, *catva* and *ṣatva*; the augment *aṭ*; the verbal *nighāta* accent).

#### Ṛk 13

**॥ संहितापाठः ॥**

> न॒वा॒नां न॑वती॒नां वि॒षस्य॒ रोपु॑षीणां ।

### Printed p. 365

> सामुक्तानां गंगादिनदीनां नामाग्रभं । गृह्णामि । संकीर्तयामि ॥ गृहेश्चांदसे
> लुजि छांदसश्चेर्लुक् । हृग्रहोर्भः ॥ अस्य योजनमित्यादि गतं ॥

*Gist:* I recite the names of the ninety-nine poison-destroying rivers, Ganges and others; the sun though far neutralises the poison; honey-lore turns it into nectar.

**प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)**

नवानां नवतीनां—तॊंभत्तॊंभत्तु संख्यॆयुळ्ळवू (*navānāṃ navatīnāṃ—tòṃbhattòṃbhattu saṃkhyèyuḷḷavū*) (those of ninety-nine in number). विषस्य—विषद (*viṣasya—viṣada*) (of poison). रोपु- षीणां—नाशकगळू आद (*ropu- ṣīṇāṃ—nāśakagaḷū āda*) (and destroyers). सर्वासां—गंगादिसकलनदिगळ (*sarvāsāṃ—gaṃgādisakalanadigaḷa*) (of all the rivers beginning with the Ganges). नाम—पवित्रवाद नामवन्नु (*nāma—pavitravāda nāmavannu*) (the sacred name). अग्रभं—स्तुतिसुत्तेनॆ (*agrabhaṃ—stutisuttenè*) (I praise). आरे—दूरदल्लिद्दरू सह (*āre—dūradalliddarū saha*) (even though far away). हरिष्ठाः—अश्वारूढनाद सूर्यनु (*hariṣṭhāḥ—aśvārūḍhanāda sūryanu*) (the sun mounted on horses). अस्य— ई विषद (*asya— ī viṣada*) (of this poison). योजनं—संपर्कवन्नु हॊंदिदनु ( ऎलै विषवे ) (*yojanaṃ—saṃparkavannu hòṃdidanu ( èlai viṣave )*) (came into contact (O poison)). मधुला—मधुविद्यॆयु (*madhulā—madhuvidyèyu*) (the honey-lore). त्वा—निन्नन्नु (*tvā—ninnannu*) (you). मधु चकार—अमृतवन्नागि परिवर्तिसिदॆ (*madhu cakāra—amṛtavannāgi parivartisidè*) (has turned into nectar).

*[As supplied, the label line of the Bhāvārtha reads धनाथ (*dhanātha*); standard label inserted. Three readings, one in the Pada of Ṛk 13 and one each in the Saṃhitā and Pada of Ṛk 14, are marked with a query, as they differ from the other lines.]*

**भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)**

I praise the sacred name of all the rivers beginning with the Ganges, ninety-nine in number and destroyers of poison. Even though far away, the sun mounted on horses came into contact with this poison. O poison, the honey-lore has turned you into nectar.

**Printed English translation**

I recite the names of ninety and nine (rivers), the destroyers of poison; although afar off, (the Sun), drawn by his coursers. will overtake the poison : the science of antidote has converted you, (Poison), to ambrosia.

**Viśeṣaviṣayagaḷu (Special Topics, Ṛk 13)**

So far the means of removing poison have been stated; now the sage describes that, for the removal of the defect of poison, he will remember the holy rivers such as the Ganges.

नवानां नवतीनां-इल्लि नवानां नवतीनां ऎंदरॆ नवाधिकानां नवतिसंख्या- कानां नदीनां (*navānāṃ navatīnāṃ-illi navānāṃ navatīnāṃ èṃdarè navādhikānāṃ navatisaṃkhyā- kānāṃ nadīnāṃ*): that is, they have said "ninety-nine rivers". In the Ṛgveda there are many places where, to mean "many" or "numerous", the words नवनवति (*navanavati*), शत (*śata*) and सहस्र (*sahasra*) are used. In such places the number need not be much considered. The sage has said that he will remember many (a great number of) holy rivers, the Ganges and others.

**Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā** (grammar page for Ṛk 13, noted briefly)

The page explains: नवानाम् (*navānām*) (by the rule षट् त्रिचतुर्भ्योहलादिः (*ṣaṭ tricaturbhyohalādiḥ*) (पा. सू. ६-१-१७९ (*pā. sū. 6-1-179*)) this word ending in *n* has the name *ṣaṭ*, so the following case ending *nām* takes the acute).

(The grammar page of Ṛk 13 continues.) नवतीनाम् (*navatīnām*) (by the rule पंक्ति विशंति (*paṃkti viśaṃti*) (पा. सू. ५-१-६० (*pā. sū. 5-1-60*)) the suffix *ti* after the word *navan*; the elision of the *n* is irregularly formed; as before the case ending *nām* in the genitive plural takes the acute); अग्रभम् (*agrabham*) (root ग्रह उपादाने (*graha upādāne*); *luṅ* in the sense of the present in the Veda; first person singular, *am* substituted for *mi*; in the Veda *luk* for *cli*; by the rule हृग्रहोर्भश्चंदसि (*hṛgrahorbhaścaṃdasi*) *bh* substituted for the root's *h*; the augment *aṭ* for the stem; the verbal *nighāta* accent because it follows a verb form).

#### Ṛk 14

**॥ संहितापाठः ॥**

> त्रिः स॒प्त म॑यू॒र्यः॑ स॒प्त स्वसा॑रो अ॒ग्रुवः॑ ।
> तास्ते॑ वि॒षं वि ज॑भिर [?] उद॒कं कुं॒भिनी॑रिव ॥ १४ ॥

**॥ पदपाठः ॥**

> त्रिः । सप्त । मयूर्यः । सप्त । स्वसारः । आग्रुवः [?] ।
> ताः । ते । विषं । वि । जभ्रिरे । उदकं । कुंभिनीःऽइव ॥ १४ ॥

**॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥**

> त्रिः सप्तैकविंशतिसंख्याका मयूर्यो मयूरस्त्रियः : ता विषकारिसर्प-
> द्वेषिण्य इति प्रसिद्धा नागद्वेषिगरुडपक्षादुत्पन्नत्वात् । तथा सप्तैतत्संख्याकाः सर्पण-
> स्वभावाः स्वसारः स्वयणेव सरणा आग्रुवः । नदीनामैतत् । सुरगंगाद्याः प्रसिद्धाः
> सप्त नद्यः संति । तास्ते हे देह तव विषं वि जभ्रिरे । विशेषेण हरंतु । तत्रदृष्टांतः।
> उदकं कुंभिनीः कुंभिन्यः कुंभवत्यः कुंभेन जलहारिण्य इव । ता यथा तद्धरंति
> तद्वन्नद्यो मयूर्यश्चातिप्रभूतं हरंतु ॥

*Gist:* Twenty-one pea-hens and seven streaming rivers, such as the divine Ganges, carry off your poison as women with pitchers carry water.

**प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)**

(देह—ऎलै देहवे) त्रिः सप्त—एकविंशतिसंख्याकवाद (*(deha—èlai dehave) triḥ sapta—ekaviṃśatisaṃkhyākavāda*) ((O body) twenty-one in number). मयूर्यः—हॆण्णु नविल गळू (*mayūryaḥ—hèṇṇu navila gaḷū*) (pea-hens). सप्त—सप्तसंख्याकवादवू (*sapta—saptasaṃkhyākavādavū*) (seven in number). स्वसारः—प्रवहिसुवुवू आद (*svasāraḥ—pravahisuvuvū āda*) (flowing ones). ताः अग्रुवः—गंगादि नदिगळू सह (*tāḥ agruvaḥ—gaṃgādi nadigaḷū saha*) (those rivers, the Ganges and others, too). कुंभिनीः—कुंभगळिंद उदकवन्नु हॊरतक्क स्त्रीयरु (*kuṃbhinīḥ—kuṃbhagaḷiṃda udakavannu hòratakka strīyaru*) (women who carry water in pitchers). उदकं इव—नीरन्नु तुंबिकॊंडु होगुवंतॆ (*udakaṃ iva—nīrannu tuṃbikòṃḍu hoguvaṃtè*) (as they carry water filled). ते—निन्न (*te—ninna*) (your). विषं—विषवन्नु (*viṣaṃ—viṣavannu*) (poison). वि जभ्रिरे—पूर्णवागि अपहरिसलि (नाशपडिसलि). (*vi jabhrire—pūrṇavāgi apaharisali (nāśapaḍisali).*) (may they carry off completely (destroy)).

### Printed p. 367

*Running head (as supplied): [अ. २. अ ५. व. १६ ] ऋग्वेदसंहिता 367 (*[a. 2. a 5. va. 16 ] ṛgvedasaṃhitā 367*).*

*(Continuation of Ṛk 14 of Sūkta 191, after the Pratipadārtha which ended the previous window.)*

**भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)**

O body, may the twenty-one peahens, and the seven rivers, the Ganges and others, that flow, carry off your poison completely, as women who carry water in pitchers carry away the water they have filled.

**Printed English translation**

May the thrice-seven peahens, the seven-sister rivers, carry off, (O Body), your poison as maidens, with pitchers, carry away water.

**Viśeṣaviṣayagaḷu (Special Topics, Ṛk 14)**

त्रिः सप्त मयूर्यः (*triḥ sapta mayūryaḥ*): मयूर (*mayūra*) means a peacock; मयूरि (*mayūri*) means a peahen; twenty-one kinds (with twenty-one varieties of species) of peahens. It is said that these peacocks arose from the garuḍa birds that hate snakes. Therefore it is well known that these peacocks fearlessly kill and eat snakes.

सप्त स्वसारो आग्रुवः (*sapta svasāro āgruvaḥ*): स्वसारः (*svasāraḥ*) means of a flowing nature, streaming. The word अग्रुवः (*agruvaḥ*) is read among the names of fingers (नि. ३-९ (*ni. 3-9*)) and among the names of rivers (नि. २-२४ (*ni. 2-24*)). Here the meaning is rivers; it is said that flowing rivers have the power to remove poison. Therefore the bhāṣyakāra has here said "the seven rivers beginning with the Ganges"; or it may be the Ganges and its tributaries. Although there are many holy rivers, since the word सप्त (*sapta*) is used here, the reliance of the sage is on seven chief rivers.

ते विषं (*te viṣaṃ*): the word "your" is addressed to the body, according to the bhāṣyakāra's explanation. It prays that the female peacocks and the seven flowing rivers may remove the poison of your (the body's) self.

उदकं कुंभिनीरिव—कुंभिनीः कुंभिन्यः कुंभवत्यः कुंभेन जलहारिण्य इव । ता यथा तद्धरंति तद्वन्नद्यो मयूर्यश्चातिप्रभूतं हरंतु (*udakaṃ kuṃbhinīriva—kuṃbhinīḥ kuṃbhinyaḥ kuṃbhavatyaḥ kuṃbhena jalahāriṇya iva | tā yathā taddharaṃti tadvannadyo mayūryaścātiprabhūtaṃ haraṃtu*): कुंभिनी (*kuṃbhinī*) means women who carry a pot (गडिगॆ (*gaḍigè*) or बिंदिगॆ (*biṃdigè*)) to bring water. As such women take water in a pot from a river or other reservoir, so may the rivers wash away the poison spread in the body: thus the example is given.

*[As supplied, the label line of the grammar page reads व्याकरणिप्रक्रिया (*vyākaraṇiprakriyā*); standard label inserted.]*

**Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā** (grammar page for Ṛk 14, noted briefly)

The page explains: मयूर्यः (*mayūryaḥ*) (the word printed मयारशब्द (*mayāraśabda*); in the feminine, since it denotes a species, जीष् (*jīṣ*); before *jas* *yaṇ* is substituted; since *yaṇ* replaces an acute, the following syllable takes the svarita).

*Running head (as supplied): [368 सायणभाष्यसहिता [मं. १ अ. २४. सू. १९१] (*[368 sāyaṇabhāṣyasahitā [maṃ. 1 a. 24. sū. 191]*).*

(The grammar page of Ṛk 14 continues.) जभ्रिरे (*jabhrire*) (root हृञ् हरणे (*hṛñ haraṇe*); *liṭ* in the sense of the imperative in the Veda; the substitute इरेच् (*irec*) for the third person plural; because it is treated as marked *k* (कित्वातिदेश (*kitvātideśa*)), *guṇa* does not occur; *yaṇ*; the verbal *nighāta* accent because it follows a verb form); कुंभिनीः (*kuṃbhinīḥ*) (कुंभः आसामस्ति इति कुंभिनीः (*kuṃbhaḥ āsāmasti iti kuṃbhinīḥ*); the suffix इनिप्रत्यय (*inipratyaya*) in the possessive sense; because the stem ends in *n* in the feminine, जीप् (*jīp*); by the first-syllable acute of the suffix *ini* the word becomes accented in the middle; in the Veda, when *jis* (as printed) follows, lengthening to the similar vowel).

#### Ṛk 15

**॥ संहितापाठः ॥**

> इ॒य॒त्त॒कः कु॑षुंभ॒कस्त॒कं भि॑न॒द्मृश॑ना [?] ।
> ततो॑ वि॒षं प्र वा॑वृते॒ परा॑ची॒रनु॑ सं॒वतः॑ ॥ १५ ॥

**॥ पदपाठः ॥**

> इयत्तकः । कुषुंभकः । तकं । भिनद्मि । अश्वना [?] ।
> ततः । विषं । प्र । ववृते । पराचीः । अनु । संवतः ॥ १५ ॥

**॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥**

> इयत्तकः कुत्सितेयत्तः । अल्पप्रमाण इत्यर्थः । कुषुंभकः कुं पृथ्विं
> सुंभति विलिखतीति सर्पाणां कुत्सितं सुंभयिता निग्रहीता कुषुंभको नकुलः ।
> स ते विषं हरत्विति शेषः । यदि न तथा स करोति तकं कुत्सितं तं नकुलमश्मना
> भिनद्मि । विदारयामि । विषनिर्हरणप्रयोगे यावद्विषापगमं तं पाषाणानुघात-
> मनुतिष्ठंति तद्विदः । तदिदमत्तोक्तं । तत एवं प्रयोगे सति विषं प्र वावृते ।
> विषावृताद्देहाद्विषं प्रवर्तते । निर्गच्छतु । काः प्रति । उच्यते । पराचीः परागंच-
> नवतीरतिदूरगाः संवतः संविभागवतो दिशोऽनु लक्ष्मीकृत्य । दिगंतं प्रति गच्छतु न
> मां प्रति गच्छत्वित्यर्थः ॥

*Gist:* The little mongoose is asked to take the poison, else I crush it with a stone; the poison is to depart to far directions.

**प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)**

इयत्तकः—अल्पप्रमाणवुळ्ळ (*iyattakaḥ—alpapramāṇavuḷḷa*) (of small measure). कुषंभकः—मुंगसियु (ई नन्न सर्पदष्टवाद विष वन्न पहरिसलि इल्लदिद्दरॆ) (*kuṣaṃbhakaḥ—muṃgasiyu (ī nanna sarpadaṣṭavāda viṣa vanna paharisali illadiddarè)*) (the mongoose (may it remove this snake-bitten poison of mine; if not)). तकं—कुत्सितवाद आ मुंगुसियन्नु (*takaṃ—kutsitavāda ā muṃgusiyannu*) (that vile mongoose). अश्वना—कल्लिनिंद (*aśvanā—kalliniṃda*) (with a stone). भिनद्दि— (*bhinaddi—*) (I crush (the entry is divided across the page boundary)).

### Printed p. 369

*Running head (as supplied): [अ. २. अ. ५. व. १६.] ऋग्वेदसंहिता 369 (*[a. 2. a. 5. va. 16.] ṛgvedasaṃhitā 369*).*

जज्जिहाकुत्तेनॆ (*jajjihākuttenè*) (I crush: the rest of the entry). ततः—अनंतर (*tataḥ—anaṃtara*) (afterwards). विषं—विषवु (*viṣaṃ—viṣavu*) (the poison). प्र वावृते—हॊरक्कॆबरलि (*pra vāvṛte—hòrakkèbarali*) (may it come out). पराचीः— अत्यंत दूरस्थवाद (*parācīḥ— atyaṃta dūrasthavāda*) (of the very distant). संवतः—दिक्कुगळन्नु (*saṃvataḥ—dikkugaḷannu*) (the directions). अनु—लक्षिसि हॊरटुहोगलि (*anu—lakṣisi hòraṭuhogali*) (may it go off aiming at (them)).

**भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)**

May the mongoose of small measure take this snake-bitten poison of mine; if not, I will crush it with a stone. Afterwards may the poison come out and go off to the very distant regions.

**Printed English translation**

May the insignificant mungoose (carry off) your venom, (Poison), if not, I will crush the vile (creature) with a stone; so may the poison depart (from my body), and go to distant regions.

**Viśeṣaviṣayagaḷu (Special Topics, Ṛk 15)**

In this ṛk the sage hopes that the mongoose will destroy the poison.

इयत्तकः-कुत्सितेयत्तः अल्पप्रमाण इत्यर्थः (*iyattakaḥ-kutsiteyattaḥ alpapramāṇa ityarthaḥ*): that is, one with a very small bodily form, small.

कुषुंभकः--कुं पृथिवीं सुंभति विलिखतीति सर्पाणां कुत्सितं सुंभयिता निग्र- हीता कुषुंभको नकुलः (*kuṣuṃbhakaḥ--kuṃ pṛthivīṃ suṃbhati vilikhatīti sarpāṇāṃ kutsitaṃ suṃbhayitā nigra- hītā kuṣuṃbhako nakulaḥ*): कु (*ku*) means the earth (the ground); because when snakes crawl on that ground there is a mark of their movement like a crooked line drawn, कुत्सितं (*kutsitaṃ*) means snakes. Because it provokes such snakes, fights them and kills them, the mongoose is named कुषुंकभ (*kuṣuṃkabha*) (as printed), that is, *nakula* or mongoose (( the neul or or viverra Mungoose) (*( the neul or or viverra Mungoose)*), as printed). It is well known that these mongooses kill the snakes that are their natural enemies. Such a mongoose is prayed to remove the poison of the body. Here the verb हरतु (*haratu*) has to be supplied.

तकं भिनद्मि अश्वना (*takaṃ bhinadmi aśvanā*) (as printed): तकं (*takaṃ*) means तं (*taṃ*), that small or base creature. It says that if the mongoose does not remove the poison, it will crush that base creature with a stone. In the procedures for removing poison, until the poison has gone completely and the cure has come, stones are struck one against another, and here too it is done so, is Sāyaṇa's explanation.

ततो विषं प्र वावृते पराचीरनु संवृताः (*tato viṣaṃ pra vāvṛte parācīranu saṃvṛtāḥ*) (as printed): by this sentence in the second half the wish is expressed that the poison, leaving the body, may go off very far in various directions without coming back near me.

> मानकः प्रवर्तमानोऽतिशीघ्रमभिगच्छन् कुषुंभको नकुलस्तदब्रवीत् । तद्वाक्य-

(*arasaṃ—śaktirahitavādudu.*) (powerless).

**भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)**

After it had been recited in this way by the sage Agastya, the mongoose that had come quickly out of the hill approached the sage and said: "The poison of the poisonous scorpion is powerless. O scorpion, your poison has no power. It cannot do harm to anyone."

**Printed English translation**

Hastening forth at the command (of Agastya), thus spoke the mungoose.—The venom of the scorpion is innocuous, scorpion, your venom is innocuous.

*[As supplied, the label line of the Special Topics reads विशेषयगळु (*viśeṣayagaḷu*), run on after the printed English; standard label inserted.]*

**Viśeṣaviṣayagaḷu (Special Topics, Ṛk 16)**

कुषुंभकस्तत् (*kuṣuṃbhakastat*): this last ṛk (of the sūkta, or of the maṇḍala) is used in the *dadhisaktu* homa in the rite called अध्यायोपा कर्म (*adhyāyopā karma*) (as divided by the printed line break) or उत्सर्जन (*utsarjana*), as explained by the Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra in the sūtra दधिसक्तूञ्ज्होतीत्युपक्रम्य कुषुंभकस्तदब्रवीत् (*dadhisaktūñjhotītyupakramya kuṣuṃbhakastadabravīt*) (आ. गृ. सू. ३-५-५ (*ā. gṛ. sū. 3-5-5*)).

In the above *adhyāyopākarma* and *utsarjana* procedures, when the *dadhisaktu* homa is performed, the students of the Ṛgveda recite and offer the first ṛk of each maṇḍala, अग्निमाळे पुरोहितं (*agnimāḷe purohitaṃ*) (as printed) (ऋ. सं. १-१-१ (*ṛ. saṃ. 1-1-1*)), and the last ṛk of the maṇḍala, कुषुंबकस्तदब्रवीत् (*kuṣuṃbakastadabravīt*) (as printed) (ऋ. सं. १-१९१-१६ (*ṛ. saṃ. 1-191-16*)); then likewise the first ṛk of the second maṇḍala, त्वमग्ने द्युभिस्तृमाशुशुक्षणिः (*tvamagne dyubhistṛmāśuśukṣaṇiḥ*) (ऋ. सं. २-१-१ (*ṛ. saṃ. 2-1-1*)), and the last ṛk of the same maṇḍala, आवदंस्त्वं शकुने भद्रमा वद (*āvadaṃstvaṃ śakune bhadramā vada*) (ऋ सं. २-४३-३ (*ṛ saṃ. 2-43-3*)). In the same way, up to the tenth maṇḍala, they recite and offer the first and last ṛks of each maṇḍala, that is, twenty ṛks in all.

गिरेः प्रवर्तमानकः (*gireḥ pravartamānakaḥ*): it means coming out at once from the holes and the like at the foot of the hill. In the previous ṛk the sage Agastya addressed the mongoose: destroy the poison in the body, or I will crush you with a stone; as soon as he said this, the mongoose, frightened, came out at once from the hole region of the mountain, its dwelling place (printed निनासस्थान (*nināsasthāna*)), and said this (the next sentence) in order to console the sage Agastya; this is the purport.

In the matter of this sūkta the scholar Wilson ऎंब पंडितनु (*Wilson èṃba paṃḍitanu*) writes as follows:

> M. Langlois has preferred a totally different interpretation of this sukta, understanding it to allude to the state of the sky before the commencement of a sacrifice ; he, therefore, interprets ವಿಷ by darkness. Which is dispersed by the morning light, or by the rays of the sun ; On what authority this view of the intention of the hymn is founded has not been stated ; nothing of the kind is intimated by Sayana whose interpretation is confirmed by the legendary application of the hymn as related by ಶೌನಕ by the corresponding text of the ಅಥರ್ವಣ ; there are no doubt, many expressions of doubtful import, and some which are used in other places, as in the ಯಜುರ್ವೇದ, in a different acceptation ; but the interpretation given by Sayana appears to be most consistent with the general purport of the text.

*[The English quotation of the supplied text contains the Kannada words विष (*viṣa*), शौनक (*śaunaka*), अथर्वण (*atharvaṇa*) and यजुर्वेद (*yajurveda*) inside the English sentences, as supplied; the printed line-end hyphen in "understan- ding" is joined.]*

वृश्चिकस्यारसं विषमरसं वृश्चिक ते विषं (*vṛścikasyārasaṃ viṣamarasaṃ vṛścika te viṣaṃ*): this sentence was said by the mongoose for the removal of poison. In the world, when poisonous creatures such as scorpions, or poisonous snakes, bite people, they become distraught with fear that they will die. That fear, more than the poison, is effective as a cause of death. Therefore it is the custom of the wise, speaking to people bitten by a snake, to say: "Do not fear, it was not a poisonous snake, no harm comes from it, you will be cured at once", telling a lie (even though a poisonous snake has bitten) and so removing the fear. If the fear is removed, the dread of the poison spreading in the body is not so great, and there is a chance of surviving. Following this policy, the mongoose came out at once from the hole in the mountain and said to the sage Agastya, who was suffering from the suspicion of poison: "O scorpion, your poison is not sharp; it is powerless." In this sentence the repetition वृश्चिकस्य अरसं विषं (*vṛścikasya arasaṃ viṣaṃ*) is to be understood as for emphasizing the meaning of the sentence. The reason the mongoose addressed the scorpion is: "O sage Agastya, a snake has not bitten you; a scorpion with little poison may have bitten. Nothing troublesome comes from a scorpion's bite. Why do you grieve over it?" With the aim of consoling, it said that the scorpion's poison is powerless and not sharp like a snake's poison; there is no need to fear on this account; the main purport is that this was said according to the policy of the world.

**Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā** (grammar page for Ṛk 16, noted briefly)

The page explains: अब्रवीत् (*abravīt*) (root ब्रूञ् व्यक्तायां वाचि (*brūñ vyaktāyāṃ vāci*); *luṅ*, first person singular, *tip*; elision of the *i* by the rule इतश्च (*itaśca*); the augment *īṭ* by the rule ब्रुवईट् (*bruvaīṭ*) (पा. सू. ७-३-९३ (*pā. sū. 7-3-93*)); *guṇa* and *av* for the root's *u*; the augment *aṭ* for the stem; the verbal *nighāta* accent).

...will kill. O serpent, run away and take shelter in a hole in the earth. If not, I shall strike you with my staff, which is swift like the chariot of the sun, strong like the arms of Viṣṇu, and falls on its target like the Garuḍa bird. At the mere coming of Garuḍa the three worlds tremble; the whole earth with its mountains, forests and the like shakes with fear. By the force of Garuḍa's coming the sun and moon become lightless and the stars do not shine; the gods tremble with fear; the wind does not blow. Therefore, O serpent full of great poison, go far away. May it be well with you. In this matter remember the word of the sage Āstika at the time of the completion of the sacrifice of King Janamejaya. The head of any serpent that, without heeding the warning words spoken by the sage Āstika, does not go away, will split into a hundred pieces like the fruit of the *śiṃśapā* tree. O river Narmadā, salutation to you in the morning and in the night time; protect and save me from the poisonous serpent. I remember the sage of great majesty named Jaratkāru's son, born of the maiden Jaratkāru (as printed). For those who remember the name of that great sage there is no fear of poisonous serpents. Therefore, O poisonous serpent, go far away; may it be well with you. For the man who remembers Asiti, Arthasiddhi and Sunīti there is no fear of serpents whether by night or by day. And the man who remembers the five great sages Agasti, Mādhava, Mucukunda, Kapila and Āstika (as printed) sleeps happily at night, free from fear of serpents.

## Maṇḍala 2

**Opening lines of the second maṇḍala (printed as plain lines)**

> ॥ श्रीः ॥
> ॥ श्री गणेशाय नमः ॥
> अथ द्वितीयं मंडलं

> *‖ śrīḥ ‖*
> *‖ śrī gaṇeśāya namaḥ ‖*
> *atha dvitīyaṃ maṃḍalaṃ*

*[A stray garbled line of the supplied text, पि ९ ८ कॆ. (*pi 9 8 kè.*), is kept as an italic note in the Kannada text.]*

**Introduction to the second maṇḍala (Kannada)**

The Ṛgveda Saṃhitā has ten divisions. These divisions are called maṇḍalas. Mainly, the whole collection of mantras composed by, or seen by, each individual sage and his descendants (or group) has been put together and fixed as one maṇḍala. But in the maṇḍalas called १, ९, १० नॆय (*1, 9, 10 nèya*) there are many sages of different groups. In the ninth maṇḍala, although there are different sages, all the mantras bear the name of one deity, पवमानसोम (*pavamānasoma*). That is, unlike the other maṇḍalas, the mantras have not been put together according to the sages; all the mantras having Soma as the deity, seen by all the sages, have been put together and made one maṇḍala. Therefore all the mantras in that maṇḍala have one deity, पवमानः सोमः (*pavamānaḥ somaḥ*); only the sages are different. In the first maṇḍala the mantras of sages who were seers of a hundred ṛks, or somewhat more or less than a hundred, have been put together. Under the name of each sage there are about १०० (*100*) ṛks. Therefore the sages of this maṇḍala are called शतर्चिनरु (*śatarcinaru*) (those who composed a hundred ṛks), and this maṇḍala is called शतर्चिनमंडल (*śatarcinamaṃḍala*).

Following this same order, for the maṇḍalas 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8नॆय (*2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8nèya*) the sages Gṛtsamada, Viśvāmitra, Vāmadeva, Atri, Bharadvāja, Vasiṣṭha and Kaṇva respectively are said to be the seers (the print has द्रष्टगळॆंदु (*draṣṭagaḷèṃdu*)). In the tenth maṇḍala many large sūktas and very small sūktas that could not be classified in any way are included; all of them are put together in this maṇḍala, and it is called the maṇḍala of small sūktas and great sūktas. As in the first maṇḍala, in this tenth maṇḍala too there are in all १९१ (*191*) sūktas (as printed). For the second maṇḍala now in hand, since the sage Gṛtsamada is the seer, it is customary to call this maṇḍala गार्त्सद मंडल (*gārtsada maṃḍala*). In every maṇḍala there are divisions called *anuvākas*, each containing several sūktas, according to the sage or the division of subject. In the first maṇḍala there are २४ (*24*) such anuvākas and in all १९१ (*191*) sūktas. In this second maṇḍala there are ४ (*4*) anuvākas and in all ४३ (*43*) sūktas. This maṇḍala is smaller in size than all the maṇḍalas.

### Printed p. 376

*Running head (as supplied): [376 सायणभाष्यसहिता [मं २. ४. १. सू. १.] (*[376 sāyaṇabhāṣyasahitā [maṃ 2. 4. 1. sū. 1.]*).*

Let us examine carefully the matter of the sage Gṛtsamada, the seer of this maṇḍala. The great sage Yāska, giving in his Nirukta the etymology of the word *gṛtsamada*, says:

गृत्समदो गृत्समदनः । गृत्स इति मेधाविनाम । गृणातेः स्तुतिकर्मणः । (*gṛtsamado gṛtsamadanaḥ | gṛtsa iti medhāvināma | gṛṇāteḥ stutikarmaṇaḥ |*)
(नि. ९-५) (*(ni. 9-5)*)

That is: *gṛtsamada* means *gṛtsamadana*; the word *gṛtsa* is derived from the root *gṛṇāti*, which gives the sense of the act of praise; he has said that the word *gṛtsa* is a name for *medhāvī* (an intelligent man). The word *madana* means one who is joyful or has joy. The analysis of the compound is गृत्सश्चासौ मदनश्च गृत्समदनः (*gṛtsaścāsau madanaśca gṛtsamadanaḥ*). Therefore the word *gṛtsamada* means a man who is intelligent and joyful (smiling-faced).

This sage Gṛtsamada was at first the son of a sage named Śunahotra, born in the line of the sage Aṅgiras. Once, while he was performing a sacrifice, asuras came and carried him off. At Gṛtsamada's prayer Indra rescued him and brought him back. By Indra's command the name Gṛtsamada became established for him. And he became known as the son of Śunaka or Śaunaka of the Bhṛgu family. And in the work called ऋष्यन-क्रमणिकॆ (*ṛṣyana-kramaṇikè*) (as printed), composed by the great sage Kātyāyana, a pupil of the sage Śaunaka, when the names of the sages of the various sūktas are given, it is said:

त्वमग्न इति गृत्समदः शौनको बृगुतां गतः । (*tvamagna iti gṛtsamadaḥ śaunako bṛgutāṃ gataḥ |*)
शौनहोत्रः प्रकृत्या तु य आंगिरस उच्यत इति ॥ (*śaunahotraḥ prakṛtyā tu ya āṃgirasa ucyata iti ‖*)

That is: although Gṛtsamada, the sage of the sūkta beginning त्वमग्ने द्युभिः (*tvamagne dyubhiḥ*), was born as the son of Śunahotra of the line of the Āṅgirasas, afterwards (for another reason) he became known as the son of Śunaka, born in the family of the sage Bhṛgu.

In the Mahābhārata there is a different history about this sage. According to the history in the Anuśāsana Parva of the Mahābhārata, King Vītahavya of the Haihaya country had a son. Because of the harassment by his enemy, Pratardana, the king of the country of Kāśī, Vītahavya gave up his kingdom, became an exile, wandered about and took shelter in the hermitage of the sage Bhṛgu. Angered by this, King Pratardana of Kāśī demanded by force that the kṣatriyas who were in the hermitage of Bhṛgu be handed over to him; then the sage Bhṛgu, not willing to give up the king who had sought refuge, said that there was no kṣatriya in his hermitage. Because he said so, so that the word of the sage Bhṛgu might not become untrue, Vītahavya became a brāhmaṇa. His son Gṛtsamada became a famous sage and became the seer of the second maṇḍala of the Ṛgveda (the supplied text ends here, at the end of the window).

### Printed p. 377

*Running head (as supplied): [आ. २. अ. ५. व. १७] ऋग्वेदसंहिता 377 (*[ā. 2. a. 5. va. 17] ṛgvedasaṃhitā 377*), as printed.*

*(Continuation of the introduction to the second maṇḍala, in the history of the sage Gṛtsamada.)*

In the Mahābhārata, in another place: when the war of the gods and the asuras took place and the gods were defeated, Indra disappeared into a secret place; while the asuras were lying in wait to kill him, Gṛtsamada took on the disguise of Indra, deceived the asuras, and thereby helped Indra to escape; so it is said. Besides, in the holy place called Naimiṣāraṇya, when the sages were performing for twelve years a sacrificial session (*satra*) and were passing the time hearing the Purāṇas and good stories from the Sūta-Paurāṇika named Lomaharṣaṇa, the name of Gṛtsamada is mentioned among that company of sages. But it is not clear whether he is the very Gṛtsamada who is the seer of this maṇḍala, or another sage with the name Gṛtsamada. And it is also known that in the branches (*śākhās*) of the Atharvaveda Gṛtsamada is one of the founders of a branch. The bhāṣyakāra Sāyaṇa has indicated this matter here and there.

In the first sūkta of this maṇḍala, seen by the sage Gṛtsamada, there are १६ (*16*) ṛks. Except for the one last ṛk, a concluding one that prays for wishes, the remaining १५ (*15*) ṛks all begin with words that denote "you", such as त्वं त्वां (*tvaṃ tvāṃ*). Not only that, in many ṛks every pāda begins with the word for "you". Sūktas with such alliteration are many in the Ṛgveda. In the ३१ नॆय (*31 nèya*) sūkta of the first maṇḍala also, as in the present sūkta, many ṛks begin with the word त्वं (*tvaṃ*). In some sūktas all the ṛks begin with the word एतच्छ (*etaccha*) (as printed). In the sūktas ३, १५, २२, २७ २८, ३८ (*3, 15, 22, 27 28, 38*) and so on of the ninth maṇḍala every ṛk begins with the word एतच्छब्द (*etacchabda*) (as printed); in some sūktas, that is, in the ३७ ने (*37 ne*) sūkta of the ninth maṇḍala, every ṛk begins with the word तच्चशब्द (*taccaśabda*) (as printed), and in that with the word सः (*saḥ*). In the same maṇḍala, in the १४ नॆय (*14 nèya*) sūkta seen by the sage Gṛtsamada, every ṛk (except the last ṛk) begins with the word अध्वर्यवः (*adhvaryavaḥ*). And in the २५ नॆय (*25 nèya*) sūkta of this same maṇḍala the last pāda of every ṛk ends like a refrain with यंयं युजं कृणुते ब्रह्मणस्पतिः (*yaṃyaṃ yujaṃ kṛṇute brahmaṇaspatiḥ*). In this way mantras and sūktas bound by various kinds of alliteration have been composed with the aim of singing, and they also show the composing skill and eloquence of the sages. In the present maṇḍala too the sage Gṛtsamada has praised various deities with ṛks and sūktas full of various alliterations and of meaning. There is no need to say that all such mantras belong to the class of very mature poetry.

#### Sūkta 1 (Maṇḍala 2)

ऎरडनॆय मंडलदल्लि मॊदलनॆय सूक्तवु (*èraḍanèya maṃḍaladalli mòdalanèya sūktavu*) ("the first sūkta in the second maṇḍala").

*[A stray line of the supplied text, :Q: (*:Q:*), is kept as an italic note in the Kannada text.]*

**Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya** (introduction)

> शतर्चिनां प्रथमं मंडलं व्याख्यातं । अथ गार्त्समदं द्वितीयं मंडलं
> व्याख्यायते । त्वमग्ने द्युभिरित्यादिकं द्वितीयं मंडलं । चत्वारोऽनुवाकाः ।
> तेषु प्रथमेऽनुवाक एकादश सूक्तानि । तत्र त्वमग्ने द्युभिरिति षोडशर्च० प्रथमं
> सूक्तं । मंडलद्रष्टा गृत्समद ऋषिः । स च पूर्वमांगिरसकुले शुनहोत्रस्य पुत्रः
> सन् यज्ञ कालेऽसुरैर्गृहीत इंद्रेण मोचितः । पश्चात्तद्वचनेनैव भृगुकुले शुनक-
> पुत्रो गृत्समदनामाभूत् । तथा चानुक्रमणिका । य आंगिरसः शौनहोत्रो
> भूत्वा भार्गवः शौनकोऽभवत्स गृत्समदो द्वितीयं मंडलमपश्यदिति । तथा तस्यॆव
> शौनकस्य वचनमृष्यनुक्रमणे । त्वमग्न इति गृत्समदः शौनको बृगुतां गतः । शौन-
> होत्रः प्रकृत्या तु य अंगिरस उच्यत इति । तस्मान्मंडलद्रष्टा शौनको गृत्समद
> ऋषिः । जगती छंदः । मंडलादिपरिभाषयाग्नॆयं । अत्रानुक्रमणिका । त्वमग्ने
> जागतं त्विति ॥ प्रातरनुवाकाशिनशस्त्रयोर्जागते छंदसीदमादिसूक्तद्वयस्य विनि-
> योगः । त्वमग्ने द्युभिरिति सूक्ते । आ. ४-१३ । इति सूत्रितत्वात् ॥ उपाकरणोत्सर्ज-
> नयोरप्याद्या विनियुक्ता ॥

*Gist:* The second maṇḍala, of Gṛtsamada, has four anuvākas; the first has eleven sūktas; the first sūkta has sixteen ṛks, to Agni, in Jagatī metre.

**Anuvāda (Kannada)** of Sāyaṇa's introduction to Sūkta 1 of Maṇḍala 2. The first maṇḍala, seen by the sages called शतर्चिनरॆंब (*śatarcinarèṃba*) (the word printed), has been explained; now the second maṇḍala, seen by the sage Gṛtsamada, is explained. The second maṇḍala begins with the sūkta त्वमग्नेद्युभिः (*tvamagnedyubhiḥ*) (as printed). In this maṇḍala there are four anuvākas. Among them, in the first anuvāka there are eleven sūktas; among those sūktas, त्वमग्ने म्यभिः (*tvamagne myabhiḥ*) (as printed, a misreading of the same words) is the first sūkta. It has sixteen ṛks. Gṛtsamada, the seer of the maṇḍala, is the sage of this sūkta; this sage Gṛtsamada, first born as the son of Śunahotra in the Aṅgiras family, was once, while performing a sacrifice, carried off by asuras and then rescued by Indra. Afterwards, according to Indra's word, he became the son of the sage named Śunaka in the Bhṛgu family and famous by the name Gṛtsamada. In the Anukramaṇikā:

य अंगिरसः शौनहोत्रो भूत्वा भार्गवः शौनकोऽभवत्स गृत्समदो द्वितीयं मंडलमपश्यदिति (*ya aṃgirasaḥ śaunahotro bhūtvā bhārgavaḥ śaunako 'bhavatsa gṛtsamado dvitīyaṃ maṃḍalamapaśyaditi*);

that is, the son of Śunahotra of the Aṅgiras gotra became, as the son of the sage named Śunaka born in the Bhṛgu family, one named Gṛtsamada. This Gṛtsamada is the seer of the second maṇḍala of the Ṛgveda, it is said. And in the Anukramaṇikā too the word of its author, Śaunaka, is as follows:

त्वमग्न इति गृत्समदः शौनको भृगुतां गतः । (*tvamagna iti gṛtsamadaḥ śaunako bhṛgutāṃ gataḥ |*)
शौनहोत्रः प्रकृत्या तु य आंगीरस उच्यत इति ॥ (*śaunahotraḥ prakṛtyā tu ya āṃgīrasa ucyata iti ‖*)

### Printed p. 379

*Running head (as supplied): [आ २. आ ५. व. १७. ] ऋग्वेदसंहिता 379 (*[ā 2. ā 5. va. 17. ] ṛgvedasaṃhitā 379*), as printed.*

The sage Gṛtsamada, who was first the son of Śunahotra of the Āṅgirasa gotra and afterwards the son of Śunaka of the Bhṛgu family, is the seer of this second maṇḍala that begins with त्वमग्ने (*tvamagne*). Therefore the sage Gṛtsamada, the son of Śunaka, is the seer of the maṇḍala. The deity of the sūkta त्वमग्ने (*tvamagne*) is Agni; the metre is Jagatī. In the Anukramaṇikā it is said त्वमग्ने जागतं तु (*tvamagne jāgataṃ tu*). That at the time of reciting the morning anuvāka and the mantras of the Āśvina śastra this sūkta and the next sūkta are used for the ṛks of Jagatī metre is explained by the Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra in the sūtra त्वमग्ने द्युभिरिति सूक्ते (*tvamagne dyubhiriti sūkte*) (आ. ४-१३ (*ā. 4-13*)); and that in the rites of Adhyāyopākarma and Utsarjana the first ṛk of this sūkta is used has been told in the Anuvāda of the previous sūkta itself.
